# sysutils_firewall_rule (Resource)

Manages one firewall rule in the `filter` table, with nftables or iptables. With nftables, the rule is added to the provider's own table `inet terraform_sysutils`; with iptables, to the built-in `INPUT`, `OUTPUT` or `FORWARD` chain. The rule is tagged with a comment that holds `name`, by which it is found again, so rules added by hand or by other tools are never changed. Requires root privileges.

Each resource owns one rule, identified by its name. Rules added by hand, by the distribution or by other tools, such as firewalld, ufw or Docker, are never changed.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Allow SSH from the office network only, and reject it from everywhere else.
resource "sysutils_firewall_rule" "ssh_office" {
  name              = "ssh-office"
  family            = "ipv4"
  chain             = "input"
  protocol          = "tcp"
  source            = "192.0.2.0/24"
  destination_ports = ["22"]
  action            = "accept"
  comment           = "SSH from the office"
}

resource "sysutils_firewall_rule" "ssh_others" {
  name              = "ssh-others"
  chain             = "input"
  protocol          = "tcp"
  destination_ports = ["22"]
  action            = "reject"

  # Rules are evaluated in order, and new rules are added at the end, so the
  # reject is created after the accept.
  depends_on = [sysutils_firewall_rule.ssh_office]
}

# Drop traffic to a range of ports on one interface, for IPv4 and IPv6
# ("inet" is the default family).
resource "sysutils_firewall_rule" "block_ephemeral" {
  name              = "block-ephemeral-eth0"
  chain             = "input"
  protocol          = "udp"
  in_interface      = "eth0"
  destination_ports = ["30000-32767"]
  action            = "drop"
}

# Keep routed traffic from a container network away from a private range.
resource "sysutils_firewall_rule" "no_lan_from_containers" {
  name         = "no-lan-from-containers"
  family       = "ipv4"
  chain        = "forward"
  in_interface = "docker0"
  destination  = "10.0.0.0/8"
  action       = "reject"
}

# Force the iptables backend, for hosts managed by iptables-based tools.
resource "sysutils_firewall_rule" "icmpv6" {
  name     = "icmpv6"
  backend  = "iptables"
  family   = "ipv6"
  chain    = "input"
  protocol = "icmpv6"
  action   = "accept"
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `action` (String) What to do with matching packets: `"accept"`, `"drop"`, `"reject"`. `"reject"` answers with an ICMP port-unreachable error; `"drop"` discards the packet silently.
- `chain` (String) Chain of the rule: `"input"`, `"output"`, `"forward"`, for packets addressed to this host, sent by it, and routed through it. Changing it moves the rule.
- `name` (String) Unique name of the rule, stored in its comment as `tf-sysutils:<name>`. 1 to 48 letters, digits, `_`, `.` or `-`, starting with a letter or digit. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `backend` (String) Firewall backend: `"auto"`, `"nftables"`, `"iptables"`. `"auto"` uses nftables if the `nft` command works, and iptables otherwise; the choice is made when the rule is created and kept afterwards (see `active_backend`). Changing it to another backend moves the rule. Defaults to `"auto"`.
- `comment` (String) Free-text comment, stored in the rule's comment after the name. 1 to 64 letters, digits, single spaces or characters of `_.,:/@+=()-`.
- `destination` (String) Destination address or CIDR prefix to match, as for `source`. Omit it to match any destination.
- `destination_ports` (Set of String) Destination ports to match, such as the port of a service running on this host. Each element is a port, such as `"22"`, or a range, such as `"8000-8100"`. Requires `protocol` `"tcp"`, `"udp"` or `"sctp"`. Ports must not overlap, and there can be at most 15, where a range counts as two, the limit of iptables' `multiport` match. Omit it to match any port; an empty set is not allowed.
- `family` (String) Address family the rule applies to: `"ipv4"`, `"ipv6"`, `"inet"`. `"inet"` matches IPv4 and IPv6; with iptables it adds one rule with `iptables` and one with `ip6tables`. `source`, `destination` and the ICMP protocols require `"ipv4"` or `"ipv6"`. Defaults to `"inet"`.
- `in_interface` (String) Name of the interface the packet arrived on, such as `"eth0"`. Not allowed in the `"output"` chain. Wildcards are not supported.
- `out_interface` (String) Name of the interface the packet leaves through. Not allowed in the `"input"` chain. Wildcards are not supported.
- `protocol` (String) Layer 4 protocol to match: `"all"`, `"tcp"`, `"udp"`, `"sctp"`, `"icmp"`, `"icmpv6"`. `"icmp"` requires family `"ipv4"`, `"icmpv6"` family `"ipv6"`. Defaults to `"all"`, any protocol.
- `source` (String) Source address or CIDR prefix to match, such as `"10.0.0.0/8"` or `"2001:db8::1"`. The prefix must not have host bits set. Requires `family` `"ipv4"` or `"ipv6"`, matching the address. Omit it to match any source.
- `source_ports` (Set of String) Source ports to match. Each element is a port, such as `"22"`, or a range, such as `"8000-8100"`. Requires `protocol` `"tcp"`, `"udp"` or `"sctp"`. Ports must not overlap, and there can be at most 15, where a range counts as two, the limit of iptables' `multiport` match. Omit it to match any port; an empty set is not allowed.

### Read-Only

- `active_backend` (String) The backend that holds the rule: `"nftables"` or `"iptables"`.
- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).

## Backends

`backend = "auto"` uses nftables if the `nft` command exists and works (the kernel supports `nf_tables`), and iptables otherwise. The choice is made when the rule is created and recorded in `active_backend`; later runs keep using that backend even if the other one becomes available. Setting `backend` to the other backend moves the rule: it is removed from the old backend and added to the new one.

### nftables

The provider keeps its rules in a table of its own, `inet terraform_sysutils`, so that they can't be confused with rules of other tools and one table holds IPv4 and IPv6 rules. The table and its `input`, `output` and `forward` base chains are created as needed, as `type filter hook <chain> priority 0; policy accept;`. When the last rule of the table is destroyed, the table is deleted as well.

Every change is one nft script, which nft applies as a single transaction: the rule is replaced in place, keeping its position, or not at all.

Keep in mind how nftables evaluates several tables: each base chain on a hook sees the packet, in the order of their priorities. A `drop` or `reject` in any chain is final, but an `accept` only ends the evaluation of *its* chain. An `accept` rule of this resource therefore does not let through a packet that another table, such as firewalld's, drops. `drop` and `reject` rules work regardless of other tables.

### iptables

Rules are appended to the built-in `INPUT`, `OUTPUT` or `FORWARD` chain of the `filter` table, with `iptables` for IPv4, `ip6tables` for IPv6, and both for family `"inet"`. They are tagged with the `comment` match, and ports use the `multiport` match. Whether a rule exists is checked with `iptables -C`, and rules are deleted with `iptables -D` and their full specification as `iptables -S` prints it, never by position, so a rule of another tool can't be deleted by mistake. A changed rule is inserted at the position of the old one before that is deleted, so it keeps its place in the chain. All commands pass `-w`, waiting for the `xtables` lock rather than failing when another iptables command holds it.

Both `iptables-nft` and `iptables-legacy` work; the provider runs whichever `iptables` is on the `PATH`.

## Rule Order

Rules are evaluated in the order of their chain, and new rules are added at the end. When the order of two rules matters, such as an `accept` for some sources followed by a `reject` for all others, make the later one depend on the earlier one with `depends_on`, as in the example above. An update keeps a rule's position unless it moves to another chain or backend, or the rule was deleted outside Terraform.

With iptables, rules of other tools that come earlier in the chain take precedence. A tool that inserts its rules at the top of a chain, as Docker does for `FORWARD`, can override them.

## Name and Comment

The rule's comment is `tf-sysutils:<name>`, followed by a space and `comment` if that is set, such as `tf-sysutils:ssh-office SSH from the office`. Names are unique per host and backend: creating a resource fails if a rule with its name exists already, rather than taking it over. Import the rule instead, or remove it.

Names and comments are restricted to characters that need no quoting in nft scripts or on command lines. Every value, including interface names, addresses and ports, is validated before it is used, and the commands are run with an argument vector, never through a shell.

## Drift Detection

On refresh, the provider lists the rules of the backend (`nft -j list table`, `iptables -S` and `ip6tables -S`) and parses the ones tagged with the resource's name back into attributes:

- If the rule was changed outside Terraform, for example to another port or action, the actual values are recorded, and the plan shows an in-place update back to the configuration.
- If the rule was deleted, the resource is removed from state and the plan shows it being created again. With iptables and family `"inet"`, a rule missing from one of `iptables` and `ip6tables` shows up as a change of `family`.
- If the rule was changed in a way the attributes can't express, such as an added counter, a negated match, a different reject type, or a copy of the rule, refresh warns and the plan shows an update of `action`, which replaces the rule with the configured one and removes the copies.

Addresses are compared as addresses, so a `source` of `"10.0.0.1"` matches the `10.0.0.1/32` that iptables prints, and the configured spelling is kept.

## Persistence

Firewall rules live in the running kernel only. After a reboot, the next plan shows the rules being created again. To have them in place at boot, before Terraform runs, save the rule set with your distribution's mechanism, such as `nft list ruleset > /etc/nftables.conf` with the `nftables` service or `netfilter-persistent save` from `iptables-persistent`. Services such as firewalld or ufw may also flush the rule set when they are reloaded; the next apply adds the rules again.

## Concurrency

Every create, update and destroy takes the provider's firewall lock (see [Concurrency and Locking](../index.md#concurrency-and-locking)) from before it lists the rules until after it has changed them, so many rules can be applied in parallel, by one or several Terraform runs.

## Import

An existing rule, typically one created by this resource in another state, can be imported by its name. With `backend = "auto"`, every available backend is searched, and the import fails if both have a rule with the name; name the backend explicitly then:

```shell
# By name, looking in every available backend.
terraform import sysutils_firewall_rule.ssh_office ssh-office

# With an explicit backend: <backend>:<name>.
terraform import sysutils_firewall_rule.icmpv6 iptables:icmpv6
```

Only rules that carry the provider's tag can be imported, and only if the attributes can express them.

## Caveats

- Requires root, or at least `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, and the `nft` command or the `iptables` and `ip6tables` commands.
- The resource changes the running host's firewall, not files below the provider's `root_dir`, so it refuses to plan when `root_dir` is set.
- Only the `filter` table is supported: no NAT, no `raw` or `mangle` tables, no connection-tracking state matches, no logging, and no interface wildcards. Use [`sysutils_exec`](./exec.md) or a file with an nft script for anything more elaborate.
- One address or prefix per `source` and `destination`; use one resource per address, for example with `for_each`.
- At most 15 ports per set, counting a range as two, as iptables' `multiport` match allows.
- The ICMP protocols match all ICMP types, and `reject` answers with ICMP port unreachable (for TCP too, rather than a TCP reset).
- The resource only works on Linux.
